screens.title: Scriptable Render Pipelines (SRPs)
screens.narratorSegment: Scriptable Render Pipelines are Unity's modern way of letting projects define how the engine renders each frame. Instead of one fixed renderer, SRPs expose rendering as a configurable pipeline you can tailor. The two primary SRPs are the Universal Render Pipeline and the High Definition Render Pipeline. URP focuses on scalability and performance across many platforms including mobile and VR; it gives a consistent, optimized feature set and makes it easier to ship broadly. HDRP targets high-end platforms and prioritizes physically accurate lighting, volumetrics, and advanced effects for realistic visuals. A concrete example: an indie mobile title will usually gain more by using URP to reduce G P U cost, while a PC architectural visualization team will likely use HDRP to access advanced lighting and materials. A common misconception is thinking HDRP always looks better in every context. In reality, HDRP provides tools for realism but demands more G P U headroom and a careful setup, and it may not run acceptably on lower-end hardware. Keep in mind that migrating between pipelines requires converting assets and shaders to the pipeline's formats. The core insight is that SRPs let you choose the right balance of features and performance for your game's goals.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Scriptable Render Pipelines
Definition

What SRPs are

SRPs turn rendering into a configurable pipeline so projects can choose different rendering behaviors and features suited to their goals.

Universal Render Pipeline (URP)
Scalable and optimized for many platforms, balancing quality and performance.
High Definition Render Pipeline (HDRP)
Engineered for high-end realism with advanced lighting and effects on powerful hardware.
Key Takeaway

Pick the pipeline that matches your performance target and desired feature set; migrating later requires asset conversion.

Example & Misconception
Example scenario: For a mobile puzzle game, URP will likely deliver smoother frame rates and simpler workflows. For a desktop photo-real demo, HDRP enables volumetrics, advanced reflection, and high-quality shadows at a higher cost.
Common Misconception
HDRP is not a universal improvement; it offers more features but requires stronger hardware and pipeline-specific assets.
Practical note
Converting projects requires creating a pipeline asset and updating materials; test early to avoid rendering surprises.
Check your understanding
If your target includes low-end mobile and PC, which pipeline is usually the safer default and why?

screens.title: URP vs HDRP — Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between URP and HDRP is about setting expectations for visuals, performance, and development cost. URP is optimized for performance and broad compatibility: it supports many platforms including mobile and VR and typically offers faster frame rates with fewer advanced lighting features. HDRP is designed for high-end visuals, with physically based lighting, volumetrics, and more sophisticated shadowing. A practical decision pattern is to start with your target platform and visual priority. If you aim for maximum aesthetic fidelity on powerful PCs or consoles — HDRP is a good fit. If you need to reach many devices or maintain high frame rates on modest hardware — URP is the better choice. A concrete example: an indie 3D platformer targeting desktop and mobile should prefer URP to avoid overtaxing phones, while an architectural visualization demo for desktop workstations can justify HDRP. Watch out for asset conversion: materials and some post-processing features differ and may need manual updates. When in doubt, prototype a scene in URP first; you can validate lighting and post-processing faster and avoid the steep optimization curve HDRP demands. URP vs HDRP — Trade-offs means base your pipeline choice on target devices and the acceptable performance budget: urp for scale, hdrp for fidelity.. In practical terms, how to choose the right pipeline for your project goals. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › URP vs HDRP
URP

Performance-first

URP favors speed and compatibility across platforms. It is the common choice for multi-platform projects and titles that need predictable performance.

Good for mobile, VR, and cross-platform builds.
Less setup complexity and lower GPU cost than HDRP.
Requires converting materials to URP formats during migration.
HDRP

Fidelity-first

HDRP unlocks advanced lighting, PBR quality, volumetrics, and high-quality shadows. It targets powerful hardware where visual realism is the priority.

Great for AAA visuals and professional renderings.
Higher GPU cost and more pipeline-specific setup.
Not suitable for low-end mobile platforms.

screens.title: Post-Processing Effects
screens.narratorSegment: Post-processing effects are full-screen image operations applied after a frame has been rendered. They let you simulate camera behavior and adjust the final look without changing scene geometry. Typical effects include Bloom to simulate light bleeding, Ambient Occlusion to darken crevices and give depth, Color Grading to shift palette and mood, Vignette to subtly darken edges, and Depth of Field to simulate camera focus. A concrete example: adding a mild Bloom plus warm Color Grading can turn a neutral scene into a soft, cinematic atmosphere. However, every effect has a cost — Ambient Occlusion and certain high-quality Bloom techniques can be G P U-heavy. A common mistake is enabling many effects at high quality without profiling; the result is a G P U-bound frame and poor performance on target devices. In URP and HDRP you add a Volume component with a Volume Profile that contains specific overrides; this modular approach makes it easy to tweak and test settings. The right approach is to pick two or three effects that serve the artistic goal, tune them modestly, and measure their performance impact. Which effect will best serve your scene's mood without breaking your frame budget?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Post-Processing Effects
Core effects

Bloom • AO • Color Grading

  • Bloom: simulates light bleed, great for highlights but can blow out details if overdone.
  • Ambient Occlusion: enhances contact shadows, adds perceived depth in crevices.
  • Color Grading: shifts overall palette; a powerful tool for mood and narrative tone.
  • Vignette & Depth of Field: guide attention and create cinematic focus.
Implementation

In URP and HDRP, post-processing lives in Volume Profiles attached to Volume components. A Global Volume applies effects to the whole scene; local volumes can affect areas selectively.

Example
Create a Global Volume, add Bloom with low threshold and warm Color Grading to push a dusk-time palette. Measure the frame cost before and after to validate the change.
Common mistake

Turning on many effects at high quality without profiling leads to a GPU-bound scenario and can harm gameplay fluidity.

screens.title: Toggling a Post-Processing Volume (C#)
screens.narratorSegment: A small script can be very useful for debugging post-processing or exposing a single toggle in player settings. The provided example shows a MonoBehaviour that holds a reference to a Volume component, tracks an enabled flag, and flips that flag when the player presses a key. Programmatically enabling and disabling a Volume is safer than destroying components because it preserves the volume profile and settings for later reuse. A concrete scenario is a 'performance mode' option that disables Bloom and Ambient Occlusion to improve frame rate during gameplay. Be careful with input handling in Update: ensure the toggle uses an input event rather than polling expensive checks repeatedly. Another misconception is thinking that disabling the Volume will always halve the frame cost: some effects remain in memory and shaders may still be compiled, so measure frame time to see the actual improvement. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Post-Processing Toggle Script
Code
// Example: Basic C# script to toggle a Post-Processing Volume
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.Rendering;
using UnityEngine.Rendering.Universal;

public class PostProcessingToggle : MonoBehaviour
{
  public Volume postProcessVolume; // Assign your Global Volume here in the Inspector
  private bool effectsEnabled = true;

  void Update()
  {
    if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.P)) // Press 'P' to toggle effects
    {
      effectsEnabled = !effectsEnabled;
      if (postProcessVolume != null)
      {
        postProcessVolume.enabled = effectsEnabled;
        Debug.Log("Post-processing effects " + (effectsEnabled ? "enabled" : "disabled"));
      }
    }
  }
}
Explanation
  • This script holds a reference to a Volume and flips its enabled state when the input occurs.
  • It preserves the Volume Profile so you can re-enable effects without reconfiguring settings.
  • Use this pattern for debugging, performance presets, or quick A/B visual comparisons.
  • Always measure frame time across devices; disabling a Volume may not equal a proportional runtime reduction.
Key Takeaway

Toggles are helpful for development and can be exposed to players, but confirm their real impact with profiling tools.

screens.title: Lighting Optimization & Baking
screens.narratorSegment: Light baking moves expensive lighting calculations out of runtime by precomputing how light interacts with static geometry and storing that result in lightmaps. This is especially valuable for scenes with many static elements such as architecture or terrain. The typical workflow is to mark static objects, set lights to Baked mode, configure your bake settings, and generate lighting via the Lighting window. Baked lighting includes both direct and indirect light, and it produces high-quality shadows without paying per-frame cost. For dynamic objects that still need to react to the baked environment, use Light Probes to capture sampled indirect lighting. A concrete example: bake a city exterior so lampposts and building shadows are precomputed, then use probes along streets so pedestrians receive appropriate indirect lighting as they move. A common pitfall is baking everything without considering scale: extremely high-resolution lightmaps increase memory usage and build times, so choose a balance between resolution and quality. Finally, always test your baked results in Play Mode because light probes and mixed lighting modes can reveal subtle mismatches that require adjusting probe placement or baking settings.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Lighting Optimization
Process

Bake workflow

  1. Mark static meshes as Static in the Inspector to include them in baked lightmaps.
  2. Set lights that should be baked to Baked mode and configure intensity and color.
  3. Open Window > Rendering > Lighting and enable Baked Global Illumination.
  4. Choose Lightmap resolution and other bake parameters carefully to balance quality and memory.
  5. Click Generate Lighting and inspect lightmaps and shadows in Play Mode.
Key Takeaway

Baking reduces runtime cost of complex lighting — choose resolutions that fit your memory and visual needs.

Why bake?
Precomputing replaces per-frame lighting math with texture lookups, letting you keep high-quality shadows without real-time expense.
Example
A static room can have soft indirect light baked to a lightmap, freeing the GPU for character animation and physics at runtime.
Pitfall

Oversized lightmaps increase build time and memory. Use conservative resolutions and iterate.

screens.title: Light Probes & Reflection Probes
screens.narratorSegment: Light probes and reflection probes are essential for integrating dynamic objects into a baked world. Light probes sample the indirect lighting from baked lightmaps at points in space so dynamic meshes can approximate the surrounding lighting without being fully baked. Reflection probes capture a spherical snapshot of the environment to provide plausible reflections on glossy or metallic surfaces. A common setup pattern is to scatter light probes in areas where characters move and place reflection probes near reflective surfaces. For example, in a hallway scene you might place probes along the corridor center line and reflection probes near glossy columns; a player character will pick up local indirect light and reflections as they move. One misconception is assuming probes are automatic; probe placement and density matter — too few probes produce abrupt lighting changes, too many increase bake time. Another practical note: reflection probes can use box projection and blend distances to smooth transitions. The key is to iteratively place probes, bake lighting, and test dynamic movement in Play Mode to ensure objects read believable lighting and reflections without resorting to expensive real-time calculations.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Probes: Light & Reflection
Light Probes

Light probes sample baked indirect lighting at discrete points so dynamic objects can receive believable indirect illumination without being baked themselves.

Place probes where dynamic objects travel, especially near occluders and corners.
Too few probes can cause sudden lighting pops; too many can slow bake times.
Reflection Probes

Reflection probes capture environment reflections to simulate glossy materials without real-time ray tracing.

Use box projection and blend distances to smooth transitions between probes.
Refresh probe captures when the environment changes significantly, or bake them for static scenes.
Practical example
Place probes along a corridor and near reflective surfaces; move a dynamic character through Play Mode to confirm lighting interpolation and reflection blending feel natural.

screens.title: Shaders & Shader Graph Basics
screens.narratorSegment: Shaders are small G P U programs that control how surfaces are drawn: they transform vertex positions and compute final pixel colors based on lighting, textures, and math. At a high level, vertex operations determine shape and position while fragment or pixel operations compute color, lighting, and surface response to light. Writing shaders by hand requires knowledge of HLSL or GLSL and careful attention to performance. Shader Graph offers a visual, node-based alternative where you connect nodes for textures, math operations, and lighting inputs to build materials without writing code. A concrete example is creating a simple rim lighting effect: sample world-space normal and view direction, compute a power curve to accentuate edges, and add that result to emissive color — all done with nodes in Shader Graph. Core idea

Vertex & Fragment stages

Vertex calculations transform geometry; fragment calculations determine pixel colors and lighting response. The cost mostly depends on per-pixel work and texture lookups.

Shader Graph
A node-based editor that produces shader code from visually connected nodes, making it approachable for designers and artists.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Convert to URP
Step-by-step
  1. Install Universal RP from Package Manager, then create a URP Asset and assign it in Project Settings → Graphics.
  2. Upgrade project materials to URP-compatible versions to avoid shader errors.
  3. Create a simple scene: Plane (ground), Cubes (static walls), Sphere (dynamic character).
  4. Add Directional Light and set Mode to Baked; mark static geometry as Static.
  5. Create a Global Volume with a Volume Profile; add Bloom and Color Grading overrides and tune them.
  6. Open Lighting window, enable Baked Global Illumination, and Generate Lighting.
  7. Add a Light Probe Group around travel areas and set the Sphere to use Light Probes for GI sampling.
  8. Place Reflection Probes near glossy surfaces and bake or capture them to provide reflections.
Why it matters

Following these steps yields consistent visuals and better performance by offloading lighting work to the bake process and using probes for dynamic objects.

Tip

Profile before and after enabling post-processing. Some settings are decorative but expensive; tune for your target device.

screens.title: Measuring Performance & Common Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Rendering features can look fantastic but also be a primary cause of poor frame rates. The first step in avoiding G P U-bound scenarios is measurement: use frame timing tools and the Unity Profiler to identify whether C P U or G P U is the limiting factor. When you find high G P U usage, inspect post-processing, expensive fragment shaders, many dynamic lights, and high-resolution shadowmaps. A common mistake is to assume that a single expensive effect dominates performance; often the combined cost of many medium-cost effects exceeds expectations. For example, combining Ambient Occlusion, high-quality Bloom, and multiple per-pixel shader instructions will cumulatively increase G P U load. Another pitfall is using complex shaders on many small objects; consider baking visual effects into textures or using simpler shaders for distant objects and LODs. For lighting, prefer baked solutions where possible and use mixed lighting modes strategically. Finally, iterate: profile on your lowest target hardware, apply one optimization at a time, and re-measure to confirm benefit. This process prevents chasing illusions and ensures each change yields measurable improvement. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Measuring Performance
Best Practice

Profile, act, verify

Use the Unity Profiler and frame timing to determine whether you're CPU- or GPU-bound. On GPU-bound frames, inspect post-processing and expensive shaders first.
  • Profile on target hardware — desktop profiling alone can hide mobile bottlenecks.
  • Disable effects one at a time to measure real impact.
  • Consider baking or simplifying shaders rather than adding more per-pixel math.
Common pitfalls include enabling many medium-cost effects, using high-resolution shadows for distant lights, and forgetting to use LODs.
Optimization tip: reduce shader complexity for distant or numerous objects and bake lighting where appropriate.
Key Takeaway

Measure before optimizing, change one thing at a time, and validate improvements on the hardware you care about most.

In this chapter you'll learn how to shape the visual quality and performance of your Unity projects. We'll compare the two Scriptable Render Pipelines — the Universal Render Pipeline and the High Definition Render Pipeline — and help you choose the one that fits your platform and visual goals. You'll master practical post-processing techniques like Bloom and Color Grading, and learn how to set up baked lighting, light probes, and reflection probes so static and dynamic objects look consistent without overwhelming the G P U. Finally, you will meet shaders and Shader Graph: what they do, how vertex and fragment stages work in principle, and how to build useful effects without overcomplicating your materials. A concrete example in this chapter shows a simple way to toggle post-processing for testing and player options. As you proceed, you should think about trade-offs: when realism is necessary and when performance matters more. By the end you'll be ready to pick a pipeline, add polished camera effects, and optimize lighting so your scenes look great and run smoothly. Which part matters most for your next prototype?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to make decisions about render pipelines, configure post-processing, optimize lighting for static and dynamic content, and start building shaders in Shader Graph. Specifically, you will learn to differentiate URP and HDRP and pick the right pipeline for your goals, which matters because choosing the wrong pipeline can add unnecessary complexity or limit visual fidelity. You will also implement post-processing via Volume Profiles so you can craft mood while measuring performance cost. Another objective is to optimize lighting using baked lightmaps for static geometry and light probes for moving objects; this reduces runtime lighting cost while preserving visual consistency. Finally, you will understand foundational shader concepts and use Shader Graph to create a simple custom material without writing HLSL, enabling artists to prototype effects quickly. Each objective combines conceptual understanding with practical steps so you can apply these techniques in an actual Unity project. As you study, think about the trade-offs between fidelity and performance and how each objective helps you reach a clear target for your game.

These objectives emphasize real, repeatable tasks you can perform in the editor. First, you'll convert a project to URP by installing the package, creating a URP Asset, and upgrading materials. This practical skill matters because a correct conversion prevents rendering artifacts and ensures compatibility with post-processing and Shader Graph. Second, you'll create and configure a Global Volume with a Volume Profile to apply Bloom and Color Grading. A concrete example is creating a moody, warm palette using color grading while keeping ambient occlusion minimal to control cost. Third, you'll set up baked lighting for static scene elements and place light probes around areas where the player or NPCs move. Observe how a dynamic character picks up indirect light from probes to match the baked environment. Finally, you'll build a small Shader Graph graph to add a glow or rim effect; this demonstrates the node-based approach without writing shader code. Each skill is paired with why it matters: reproducible steps save debugging time and let you iterate on visuals without unexpected performance regressions.

Scriptable Render Pipelines are Unity's modern way of letting projects define how the engine renders each frame. Instead of one fixed renderer, SRPs expose rendering as a configurable pipeline you can tailor. The two primary SRPs are the Universal Render Pipeline and the High Definition Render Pipeline. URP focuses on scalability and performance across many platforms including mobile and VR; it gives a consistent, optimized feature set and makes it easier to ship broadly. HDRP targets high-end platforms and prioritizes physically accurate lighting, volumetrics, and advanced effects for realistic visuals. A concrete example: an indie mobile title will usually gain more by using URP to reduce G P U cost, while a PC architectural visualization team will likely use HDRP to access advanced lighting and materials. A common misconception is thinking HDRP always looks better in every context. In reality, HDRP provides tools for realism but demands more G P U headroom and a careful setup, and it may not run acceptably on lower-end hardware. Keep in mind that migrating between pipelines requires converting assets and shaders to the pipeline's formats. The core insight is that SRPs let you choose the right balance of features and performance for your game's goals.

Choosing between URP and HDRP is about setting expectations for visuals, performance, and development cost. URP is optimized for performance and broad compatibility: it supports many platforms including mobile and VR and typically offers faster frame rates with fewer advanced lighting features. HDRP is designed for high-end visuals, with physically based lighting, volumetrics, and more sophisticated shadowing. A practical decision pattern is to start with your target platform and visual priority. If you aim for maximum aesthetic fidelity on powerful PCs or consoles — HDRP is a good fit. If you need to reach many devices or maintain high frame rates on modest hardware — URP is the better choice. A concrete example: an indie 3D platformer targeting desktop and mobile should prefer URP to avoid overtaxing phones, while an architectural visualization demo for desktop workstations can justify HDRP. Watch out for asset conversion: materials and some post-processing features differ and may need manual updates. When in doubt, prototype a scene in URP first; you can validate lighting and post-processing faster and avoid the steep optimization curve HDRP demands. Post-processing effects are full-screen image operations applied after a frame has been rendered. They let you simulate camera behavior and adjust the final look without changing scene geometry. Typical effects include Bloom to simulate light bleeding, Ambient Occlusion to darken crevices and give depth, Color Grading to shift palette and mood, Vignette to subtly darken edges, and Depth of Field to simulate camera focus. A concrete example: adding a mild Bloom plus warm Color Grading can turn a neutral scene into a soft, cinematic atmosphere. However, every effect has a cost — Ambient Occlusion and certain high-quality Bloom techniques can be G P U-heavy. A common mistake is enabling many effects at high quality without profiling; the result is a G P U-bound frame and poor performance on target devices. In URP and HDRP you add a Volume component with a Volume Profile that contains specific overrides; this modular approach makes it easy to tweak and test settings. The right approach is to pick two or three effects that serve the artistic goal, tune them modestly, and measure their performance impact. Which effect will best serve your scene's mood without breaking your frame budget?

Light baking moves expensive lighting calculations out of runtime by precomputing how light interacts with static geometry and storing that result in lightmaps. This is especially valuable for scenes with many static elements such as architecture or terrain. The typical workflow is to mark static objects, set lights to Baked mode, configure your bake settings, and generate lighting via the Lighting window. Baked lighting includes both direct and indirect light, and it produces high-quality shadows without paying per-frame cost. For dynamic objects that still need to react to the baked environment, use Light Probes to capture sampled indirect lighting. Let's summarize the key concepts you should carry forward. First, URP and HDRP are Scriptable Render Pipelines with different goals: URP for scalable performance across platforms, HDRP for high-fidelity visuals on powerful hardware. Second, post-processing effects like Bloom and Color Grading shape mood but cost G P U time — choose and tune effects with profiling. Third, lighting optimization through baking moves expensive lighting work out of runtime; use light probes to let dynamic objects sample the baked lighting and reflection probes to approximate environment reflections. Each concept is a trade-off: visual quality versus runtime cost. Practice these techniques in small scenes, measure the impact, and adopt the simplest solution that achieves your visual goals. Third, prefer baked lighting and probes for static scenes and dynamic objects respectively — this keeps runtime costs low while preserving believable lighting.
